text: You may have already forgotten me, but I will remind you of certain circumstances, and I believe you will remember who I am. Do you remember when you were traveling through Europe and stopped in Prague, and all the Bulgarian students treated you so coldly, even Jireček, and I was the only one who invited you to my home, where you stayed for several days? Do you remember when you caught me with the landlady’s daughter? And do you remember, when you were left alone, how they entertained you and you sang "The Night is Terrible" to them? I am that same person, Bodkov; I have finished my higher education and returned to my fatherland. Since I have no other influential person among my acquaintances besides you, I turn to you with a request and ask you to ask one of the editorial offices of a government newspaper to publish the report attached here, of which I am also sending a copy to you, in case it should be lost at the editorial office. I believe that this report is sufficient for the government to form an idea of my views; I am even capable of writing much more than this, should the need arise. I have a degree in philosophy, Mr. Balkanski! Furthermore, I have one more request for you: my father is a contractor, and they are currently rejecting fifty thousand levs' worth of shoes of his, so I would ask you to intercede so that they might accept them, just as they accepted shoes made of the same material from a Jew. Is that patriotic?

Do not think that I am writing my report to please the government. Not at all. The scrapping of the shoes has nothing to do with the report, and finally, you must know that I am not a man who trades in his convictions.
Please accept the assurances of my highest consideration.
P.S. The editors may change my report as they see fit; I am not a demanding person.
P. P. S. The shoes were written off three days ago.
Here is the report mentioned in the letter above:

My blood freezes in my veins, my brain stiffens against my skull, my heart ceases to beat, and with a trembling soul I cry out to the honorable Government and beg it to answer: will there be an end to its patience toward the destructive licentiousness of the opposition press? The people want to know (I can boldly assert this) when the sacrilegious fingers of the opposition will be broken—those who dare to touch—oh, horror!—the Virgin and Sacred Person of our common Father, the pledge of our happiness and prosperity. Instead of unquestioning, reverent bowing before the bright personification of our independence, instead of kneeling readiness to satisfy the Highest whims and desires, there appear among us Bulgarians (monsters of the Bulgarian people) who dare to attribute human weaknesses to the untouchable Person!!!... This is more than a betrayal of national interests. This is a depravity unprecedented in history! There were even such brigands of the pen who rose up and tried to stop and desecrate the greatest virtue of our municipalities, where they gift municipal forests, islands, and gardens to their Highest Favorite. The greatness of the throne is simultaneously the greatness of the people, and instead of being proud that our municipalities demonstrate their love for the Crown and the Dynasty, instead of rejoicing that our until-recently wild fatherland is being covered with luxurious palaces and villas, there are Bulgarians—imagine, Bulgarians!—who even then are not satisfied! Such malcontents sow depravity in society, and the Bulgarian people must look upon them with loathing. They are the cause of the moral decline of our society and for that mistrust which is instilled between the government and society, and which so badly affects the national livelihood. From this mistrust suffer the private interests of the most respected and conscientious merchants, as is the case with our esteemed citizen NN, whose shoes, made of the finest material and worth 50,000 BGN, were rejected these days due to a misunderstanding. And so, the Government must take measures to shut the mouths of the opposition once and for all. This is the most fervent wish of the Bulgarian people.
I promise you that in the future I will write you as many such reports against the opposition as you wish; I only ask that my name remains incognito to the public. I have graduated in philosophy.

It comes to my mind who you were, Your Grace; how could I not remember? I remember you, I remember your fiancée, and her mother was a decent soul; after all, I taught them to cook this and that, and we played the piano—I remember it very well. You’ve mastered your trade, as I see you; this philosophy, as it turns out, wasn't just for making fools out of people. And as for the shoes you wrote about, you’ve made a bit of a mistake; that business isn't settled with a newspaper report. You see, they accepted the Jew's shoes—accepted them indeed—because he knows where Abraham digs for roots; you ought to loosen your purse strings as well. I read your letter from beginning to end and understood what your struggle is, but being an entrepreneur is not a spoon for every mouth; it’s nothing like philosophy, and you should realize for yourself on whom the acceptance of your shoes depends—on your father, that is. And as for what you say about the dynasty—well, never mind, let it be; that’s just the fashion these days. After all, words break no bones.

I am addressing you, you are a representative of the people and we ask that in the future such things do not repeat themselves, where a whole regiment goes through the forest and barks like dogs and the gentlemen officers shoot rabbits, because we were not sent to learn how to bark, but to guard our fatherland and completely exhausted, worn out, tears running from your eyes, starving, yet they force you to bark, and it must be done well, like a hound, otherwise a beating, for not knowing how to bark like a hunting dog, and they killed only five (5) rabbits. It is good that they did not wound some soldier, because he would have gotten a beating again for not looking out for himself. Besides this, they appointed me as an orderly and I wash the child's underwear and the carriage as well. This is a shameful thing and we ask you to pass a law and as I have nothing more to write to you, I remain. Tear up the letter.

Aren't you the son of Trpko the Komitadji? I know your father. As for what you say about them making you bark at rabbits in the forest, I heard it too, but patience is salvation, as they say; one doesn't kick against the goad. After all, we endured under the Turks for a lifetime, what's the harm in enduring under Bulgarians for a couple of years, it's no big deal; and as for the underwear, it's not good for a man, it's women's work, but what can you do, wash the underwear and turn your head away, politics requires it so. You know what they're like, but you just blink and endure, and give my regards to your father, don't forget. Patience, there's nothing else; these things are settled with patience, not with a racket. A bowed head, you know, the sword does not strike.

I want to take our Rada to study abroad this year, and so that there are no expenses, I beg you to pull some strings with the higher-ups there to have me commissioned for something, to study some issues or for some kind of agitation: for example, I could study the issue of introducing our frieze for the Belgian army, or study the ethnography of the Koutzovlachs in Switzerland, or something similar. If they want to, they can come up with ninety-nine commissions. I am even okay with three napoleons per diem. Answer me as soon as possible.

P. S. And you won't be left without benefit from this business trip. If they ask you about my education, tell them that although I don't have a diploma, I have read a lot and it's just as if I have a higher education.
I could not find an answer to this letter in Bay Ganyo’s notebook, but in the envelope I found a draft of the following telegram:
You are very late, Vasil, another, more learned than you, has already been dispatched for these matters.

Man proposes, God disposes: all the plans we hatched for my future are shattered to pieces. My career is definitively ruined. I have been expelled from school and am doomed to three years of slavery in the convict companies, and the reason for all this is that wretched Bulgarian orthography: recently a new fashion has emerged, that we should write foreign words and names just as they were supposedly pronounced, e.g., not to write *ministr*, but to write *ministar*; not to write *ansambl*, but to write *ansambal*; not to write *Buckle*, but to write *Bukal*, because this was supposedly more characteristic of the Bulgarian language, as if the characteristic of our language were necessarily to approach Afghan. We opposed our learned mentors and they declared us rebels. On the very eve of the Nativity of Jesus Christ, the Savior of mankind, under a mounted gendarmerie convoy, we, involuntary tourists on foot, were driven along the snowy roads of Mother Bulgaria, and we march, march from stage to stage, sleep in the precincts; we are met by bailiffs, seen off by gendarmes, and where they are leading us, we ourselves do not know. They say that for the triumph of Bulgarian orthography, they found it useful to educate us for three years in the convict companies. Who knows! This miracle might happen too. I have been brought here now, to your city, and I am writing this letter from the detention room. If you please, come to see me and bring a doctor, because I do not know whether from the journey or from the cold, these past few days I have begun to spit blood.

P.S. I have heard, uncle, that the Turks had a custom for the great holidays, such as Christmas and Easter, to release the Christian prisoners on bail to see their loved ones and spend God's holidays. Is this true, uncle?

You got what you were looking for, my boy, and that’s what you found. Who’s to blame? I wonder how they didn’t give you a beating on top of it all. Of course. Are we playing with walnuts here, or are we ruling a kingdom? What is this lawlessness? Why are you rattling on to me about the Turks, saying they were more merciful. They aren’t merciful, they are fools. If they were smart, they wouldn’t have given their kingdom to someone else. If you ask me, I’m even glad that they finally caught you properly. Rot now in the precincts and barracks, so your wits come back to you, so you remember when you held your head high. I couldn’t understand from your letter what the reason was, you write to me about some sort of Buckle-Muckle, but I don’t believe you, even if I don’t understand grammar. Who knows what mischief you’ve done. I don’t have time to go around precincts compromising myself before the big shots by meeting with rebels. How many times have I taught you that a submissive head a sword does not strike. You didn’t listen to me—now break your own head. You got what you were looking for, my boy, and that’s what you found.
